newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bond investors keep nerve amid poll jitters.
newsitem.headline: French bond investors keep nerve amid poll jitters.

text.p: Investors in French bonds kept their nerve on Friday in the face of an opinion poll showing the left gaining ground in the country's parliamentary election race.
"There is still a consensus view the right will win," said economist Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon Brothers.
But some economists said the market might be over-optimistic and if more polls showed the left advancing further ahead of the May 25-June 1 vote, a fast retreat could be on the horizon.

"They are a little too hopeful," Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange said of investors. While he said he did not expect the left to win, "it astonishes me that they do not seem to have taken into account that the left could win."
Ten-year bond futures rose 22 basis points to end the day at 129.74 while the gap in yields in 10-year government bonds (OATs) over their German counterparts stayed steady.
Partly behind the market's calm, economists said, is the fact that only a small portion of domestic debt is held by outsiders, who normally sell at the first whiff of political uncertainty.
Just 12 percent of government notes and bonds are in the hands of foreigners. The big actors are domestic financial institutions, in for the longer haul.
The French bourse, held at least 30 percent by foreigners, was taking the election uncertainty harder, as shown by its underperformance against other European markets, traders said.
The CAC-40 share index closed down 0.36 percent at 2,633.91, ignoring rises on Wall Street and fresh records in London.

A win by the Socialists in the two-round vote would trigger an initial sell-off of both bonds and stocks, economists said, but they forecast the markets would recover once it became clear budget constraints would not allow the Socialists to deviate much from the policies of the centre-right.
"The market probably assumes rightly that even if the Socialists won they would remain committed to monetary union," said Mercier.

The poll by IPSOS institute released on Thursday forecast that the rightist RPR/UDF coalition would get 290 seats in the National Assembly, just one more than is needed for a majority, the Socialists and their allies would win 264 and the Communists 22 for a total of 286, just four short of the RPR-UDF tally.

It was the slimmest lead yet for Prime Minister Alain Juppe's coalition since President Jacques Chirac gambled and called the election early to give him a free hand in the runup to a single European currency to pursue his austerity policies.
The poll had the RPR-UDF taking 38 percent of the vote, the Socialists and their allies 29 percent and the Communists nine.

One dealer said the left often scored better in IPSOS polls than in those by other firms. "We have a lot of polls next week. If they confirm the Socialists gaining, the market will react negatively," said Paribas analyst Nathalie Fillet.

Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said the high degree of undecided respondents leaves the outcome uncertain. But if the percentage of those supporting the RPR-UDF fell to 35 percent, he would expect a "pretty negative" reaction by bonds.

A recent Reuter poll of economists suggested an opposition win would leave the franc more than three centimes weaker by June 15 against the mark at 3.41 against 3.3740 on Friday. French 10-year bond yields would also suffer with yields expected to climb to 20 basis points above 10-year Bund yields compared with minus nine basis points on Friday. The two-year spread would snap out to 40 from 20 on Friday if the left won.
But French and German 10-year bond yields were expected to be the same by October 15 even if the left won.
Economists said they were already detecting a move toward the centre by the Socialists in their latest declarations.

"At the start they were talking about raising business taxes. Their new manifesto doesn't talk about that and there is obviously disagreement over privatisation policy in the party," said Deutsche Bank's Mange.
